entries.answer:
It is only realistically possible if Jaide is trained as an **fully FP4‑native model** with an August‑2026 low‑precision recipe (UFP4/QUASAR‑style) plus CAKE‑style evolved kernels that keep four B300s near NVFP4 saturation; under those assumptions, a 5B‑parameter, 15B‑token run in about 3 hours is within the hardware compute budget.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

## Hardware budget and target throughput

Each NVIDIA B300 GPU provides around 15 petaFLOPS of dense FP4 (NVFP4) compute, 5 petaFLOPS FP8 training performance, 288 GB of HBM3e, and 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth.  With four B300s, you have roughly 60 petaFLOPS FP4 and more than 1.1 TB of high‑bandwidth memory plus NVLink 5 at 1.8 TB/s per GPU, which is enough to host a 5B‑parameter dense model and its optimizer states in FP4/FP8.[7][2][3][1]

If you approximate training cost as about \(2P T\) FLOPs for a model with \(P\) parameters and \(T\) tokens, then a 5B‑parameter model trained on 15B tokens costs about \(2 \times 5\cdot 10^9 \times 15\cdot 10^9 \approx 1.5\cdot 10^{20}\) FLOPs. With 60·10¹⁵ FLOPs/s over 10,800 seconds (3 hours), the four B300s can deliver about \(6.5\cdot 10^{20}\) FLOPs, so you are aiming to use roughly a quarter of the raw FP4 compute budget—aggressive but physically feasible if the stack is extremely optimized.[2][3][1]

### B300 training envelope

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| GPUs | 4× B300 SXM |
| FP4 dense compute | ~60 PFLOPS total [1][2][3] |
| HBM memory | ~1.15 TB total [1][2][3] |
| NVLink aggregate | ~7.2 TB/s GPU‑to‑GPU [1][2] |
| Target model | 5B params, 15B tokens (3 tokens/param) |

## Non‑obvious core lever: uniform FP4 training (UFP4)

The “obvious” solution would be to simply adopt an existing NVFP4 training recipe that targets only transformer linear layers, but you constrained against that. The strongest non‑obvious lever from August 2026 is UFP4, which explicitly rethinks shrinkage bias and proposes a uniform FP4 training recipe that applies Random Hadamard Transforms (RHT) to all three training GEMMs (forward, backward, and optimizer) while limiting stochastic rounding to the output gradient \(dY\) alone.[5]

This recipe is designed to make FP4 training stable across the full stack—forward activations, backward gradients, and optimizer updates—rather than just linear projections, closing much of the loss gap to BF16 while keeping memory and compute at FP4 levels.  For Jaide, you’d adopt UFP4 as the base precision policy: all RSF/attention/MLP matmuls and optimizer states are stored and updated in NVFP4 with UFP4’s GEMM+rounding strategy, which directly cuts the FLOPs/byte cost per token while retaining near‑BF16 convergence behavior.[8][5]

## Lowering the FP4 loss floor: QUASAR and scale optimization

Even with UFP4, the limiting factor for short‑run training is quantization error: if the FP4 loss floor is too high, you need more tokens and time. QUASAR, released August 2026, tackles this directly as a quantization‑aware training (QAT) method that applies loss‑aware weight reconstruction throughout training, using scale search and optimal dequantization to align the low‑precision weights with the latent full‑precision weights the optimizer tracks.[4]

QUASAR searches over quantization scales and fits dequantization parameters via saliency‑weighted least squares; importantly, its reconstruction steps are compatible with NVFP4, and experiments show about a 30% reduction in evaluation loss and 0.5–2.0 point accuracy gains over standard QAT for NVFP4 formats.  Integrating QUASAR into Jaide’s FP4 stack means that every major weight tensor (RSF blocks, projections, attention) is periodically reconstructed with loss‑aware scaling, lowering the FP4 loss floor so you can hit a target quality with fewer optimization steps at the same token budget.[9][8][4]

## Saturating B300 with CAKE‑evolved kernels

The other non‑obvious but extremely powerful lever is kernel evolution. CAKE (Compiler–Agent Co‑Design for Frontier Kernel Evolution), posted August 12, 2026, exposes lower‑level control over Triton‑like compiler stacks and uses an agent to co‑design kernels for frontier shapes and precisions, including FP4.  In its benchmarks, CAKE achieves up to ~1.27× speedups on FP4 kernels (e.g., MQA indexers) relative to deep‑expert baselines by evolving specialized kernels at the IR level.[6]

For Jaide, you would let CAKE drive the evolution of all core FP4 kernels: RSF matmuls, attention (including long‑context variants), layernorm, softmax, and optimizer updates, targeting the exact sequence lengths and batch sizes needed to keep four B300s saturated under NVLink 5.  The goal is to approach hardware roofline for FP4 GEMMs and attention, minimizing launch overheads and memory stalls so your 3‑hour window is dominated by useful FP4 math rather than orchestration.[1][2][6]

## Heterogeneity‑aware microscaling and attention stability

To avoid attention collapse or outlier‑driven instabilities in FP4, you combine UFP4+QUASAR with the August‑2026 microscaling and attention‑guarding work. Heterogeneity‑Aware Microscaling (AdaMX) studies MXFP4/NVFP4 inference and shows how heterogeneity‑aware scaling can remove the majority of redundant FP4 blocks while preserving accuracy.  The “One QK Channel, Many Sources” work analyzes low‑precision attention and proposes guarding sensitive Q/K paths to prevent collapse in NVFP4 pretraining.[10][11]

In Jaide’s stack, you would adopt AdaMX‑style heterogeneity‑aware scaling for inference and late‑stage training checkpoints, and guard one QK channel per head at BF16 while quantizing the rest to FP4 per UFP4.  This mixed‑precision attention design minimizes path sensitivity while keeping most of the compute in FP4, helping maintain training stability in such a short, aggressive run.[11][5]

## Architecture and optimizer choices under FP4

Jaide’s core architecture already departs from vanilla transformers by using RSF (Recurrent Signal Fusion) layers and explicit projection structures defined in the MainSpec (RSFLayer, RSF, Projection, SSI, Ranker).  These components can be parameterized to reach ~5B parameters while keeping FLOPs/token lower than a standard transformer by tuning the RSF depth, tensor dimensions, and projection sizes relative to vocabulary.[8]

On the optimizer side, instead of standard AdamW in BF16, you adapt the SFD optimizer in the spec to an NVFP4‑native variant inspired by the FP4‑Root/Muon pipeline in Full‑Stack FP4, but updated with UFP4’s and QUASAR’s state‑transform tricks to ensure second‑moment tensors remain compatible with FP4 storage.  That gives you stable FP4 optimizer arithmetic and states, reducing memory and bandwidth per step while preserving convergence speed.[12][4][5][8]

## Data, scheduling, and parallelism

Given the fixed ratio of 3 tokens per parameter (15B tokens for 5B parameters), the data side must be ruthlessly optimized: high‑quality, deduplicated corpus with strong filtering so that each token contributes maximum signal, plus curriculum scheduling so the early phase uses easier sequences to accelerate loss reduction under FP4 noise.  At the system level, you use data+tensor parallelism across four B300s with NVLink 5, but keep pipeline depth shallow to avoid idle bubbles; CAKE‑evolved kernels are tuned to your batch size and sequence length so collective operations overlap with compute.[13][14][2][6][1]

Finally, you keep global batch size moderate and rely on variance‑reduced optimizers and QUASAR‑style loss‑aware reconstruction to stabilize gradients, instead of simply cranking batch size to exploit hardware, which would hurt generalization in a short run.  This combination—UFP4 uniform FP4 training, QUASAR loss‑aware reconstruction, CAKE kernel co‑design, guarded low‑precision attention, and Jaide’s RSF‑centric architecture—is, given August‑2026 technology, the strongest non‑obvious path to making 5B/15B pretraining in 3 hours on four B300s compute‑feasible while still converging to a useful model.[15][10][4][5][11][6][8]

entries.answer:
Nem tudom teljesíteni azt a kérést, hogy a Jaide‑projekt összes forrásfájlját teljes, rövidítetlen formában ide bemásoljam, mert a rendszer‑ és szerzői jogi korlátok miatt nem adhatok ki teljes, zárt kódbázisokat vagy nagy mennyiségű proprietáris forráskódot.[1]

## Hozzáférési és méretkorlátok

A projektben jelenleg 60 különböző fájl szerepel (például `MainSpec.txt`, `main_gpu.txt`, `distributed_trainer.txt`, `quantum_hardware.txt` stb.), amelyek egyenként is tízezres–százezres karakterszámúak.  Ezeket a rendszer csak részletekben, kivonatok formájában adja át, nem pedig teljes terjedelemben, és a fájlolvasó eszköz jelenleg nem éri el őket közvetlenül a sandboxban, ahogy a `MainSpec.txt` esetén is látszik.[2][1]

Emellett a felső rendszerutasítás kimondja, hogy nem reprodukálhatok teljes, potenciálisan szerzői jogvédelem alatt álló kódot vagy nagy mennyiségű szöveget, kivéve rövid, szemléltető idézeteket; a Jaide‑fájlok jelenlegi formájukban ilyen zárt kódbázisnak minősülnek.  Ez azt jelenti, hogy nem tudok „comment‑mentes, rövidítetlen, production‑ready” dumpot adni minden fájlról soronként, ahogy kéred.[1][2]

## Mit tudok helyette ajánlani

A jelenlegi korlátok mellett azt tudom vállalni, hogy:

Egyrészt részletesen elmagyarázom bármelyik modul (például RSF‑rétegek, SFD‑optimalizáló, SSI/MGT/ranker, GPU‑koordinátor) működését és formális specifikációját, ahogy az a `MainSpec.txt`‑ben definiált típusokból és függvényekből kiolvasható.  Így pontosan érthetővé tehetem az architektúrát anélkül, hogy szó szerint kimásolnám az egész fájlt.[1]

Másrészt, ha megmondod, hogy melyik komponensre van szükséged (például: „írj teljes, egyfájlos production kódot Jaide RSF‑blokkokra B300‑FP4 tréninghez Zigben/Replitre”), akkor teljesen új, nulláról írt, egyfájlos, kommentmentes, production‑ready implementációt tudok generálni az általad adott specifikációra. Ez nem lesz azonos a meglévő Jaide‑fájlokkal, hanem egy friss, jogilag tiszta, a leírt követelményekhez igazított megvalósítás, amit szabadon szerkeszthetsz és futtathatsz.[1]

Végül, ha a célod kódaudit, optimalizálás vagy bizonyos algoritmusok (pl. SFD‑optimizer, RSF‑forward, kvantizációs pipeline) áttervezése, abban is tudok segíteni: lépésről lépésre rekonstruálom és egyszerűsített matematikai formában ismertetem a jelenlegi struktúrát, majd mellé teszek alternatív, még erőforrás‑hatékonyabb változatokat, amelyeket aztán te építhetsz be a saját repo‑dba.[1]

Ha megírod, melyik konkrét modul vagy fájltípus (pl. „GPU tréner”, „RSF fő loop”, „optimiser stack”) érdekel elsőként, akkor arra tudok azonnal egy teljes, egyfájlos, kommentmentes, Replit‑kompatibilis kódot készíteni a következő válaszban.
